vignette:
It happened on a Thursday evening, just after eleven. He had been walking back to his truck from a late gym session near the waterfront—a route he had taken a hundred times without a second thought. The marina was quiet, the air damp with salt and diesel. He heard footsteps behind him, but he did not turn. Coast Guard training had taught him to stay aware of his surroundings, yet that night his instincts were one beat slow. A hand grabbed his collar, yanked him sideways into the alley between two boat sheds. There were two of them, maybe three—he cannot say for sure, because his memory fractures from that point. A fist connected with his cheekbone. Another blow to his ribs. Someone shoved a knife against his throat while a second pair of hands ripped his watch off his wrist and dug through his pockets for his wallet and phone. He remembers the slick cold of the blade, the grime of the pavement against his back, the smell of sweat and stale beer. Then they were gone. He lay there for what felt like minutes, maybe longer, his breath coming in shallow, ragged bursts, before he forced himself to stand and walk, dazed, to the Coast Guard station three blocks away.

That was four months ago. Now, at twenty-nine, he is a different man. He still reports for duty at Station Fairhaven, still pulls on the orange Mustang suit, still climbs aboard the 47-foot motor lifeboat when the call comes in. But something has cracked inside him. During routine patrols, he finds himself scanning the shoreline not for distress signals but for figures in the shadows. His hand drifts toward the knife clipped to his pocket—never carried before the mugging, always carried now. When the boat idles near a dock at night, his eyes fix on the alley mouths, and his chest tightens until he can feel the ghost pressure of a blade against his throat. His crewmates have noticed. The petty officer asked if he was sleeping. He lied and said yes. He is not. He sleeps in two-hour stretches, jolting awake from dreams that are not quite replays—more like echoes: a dark shape, a hand closing, the sensation of falling. His girlfriend, Lena, has started sleeping on the couch two or three nights a week because he thrashes, once nearly hitting her in the face. She asked him to talk to someone. He told her it was fine. The truth is that he cannot talk about it. The words stick. When Lena tries to bring it up, his jaw locks, and he walks out of the room.

At work, he has become compulsively thorough. He checks the rescue gear three times before every launch, runs through emergency procedures aloud even when no one asks. It is not diligence; it is a need to control what can be controlled, because the memory of helplessness—of lying on that pavement while a stranger’s knees pinned his chest—returns without warning. Yesterday, during a routine safety briefing, the lieutenant mentioned situational awareness, and he felt the floor drop out beneath him. He had to excuse himself to the head and stand with his palms flat against the cool tile, breathing through his teeth until the shaking stopped.

He no longer goes to the gym near the marina. He takes the long way home, avoiding the waterfront entirely. On his days off, he stays inside, watches television with the volume low so he can hear footsteps outside. He has not worn his watch since the night it was taken, and he declines invitations from friends to meet for drinks, inventing reasons that sound hollow even to him. Lena asked him last week why he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind. He did not have an answer. He has not told her that sometimes, in the grocery store, a stranger’s sudden movement will send his heart into a sprint, or that he plans exit routes in every room he enters. He is a rescue swimmer. He is trained to stay calm under pressure. But the calm has frayed, and he does not know how to stitch it back together.
